storyHtml:
Type your address and see your street from above in 1928, the way a survey plane photographed it, with the same spot today below it. Most Berlin Altbau blocks were already standing, so you can often find your own courtyard. If your house is newer, you see what stood there before it.

The print carries your street, district, map coordinates and an optional line of your own.

alt: Example personalised aerial print: Spandauer Damm in West Berlin in 1979 and today
storyHtml:
Type an address in West Berlin and see your street from above in May 1979, the way a survey plane photographed it, with the same spot today below it. The Wall still divided the city then. The flight was flown over West Berlin, and along the Wall it also caught a strip of East Berlin.

If you lived in Kreuzberg, Schöneberg or Spandau then, or your parents did, you can often find your own courtyard, the street trees and the cars parked outside that spring. My advice: start with the building, then tap the photo to move the cross onto your own front door. If your address was further east in East Berlin, the preview tells you right away.

The print carries your street, district, map coordinates and an optional line of your own.

I selected this close upward view of the Siegessäule and directed the architectural corrections while keeping its angle and gouache style. The artwork was created and edited digitally, then enhanced with Adobe Firefly Upscaler. It is an artistic interpretation, not a measured architectural drawing.

Photographic inputs used in the artistic adaptation:

Kottbusser Tor: source photographs and changes

Gunnar Klack — Wohnbebauung-Kottbusser-Tor-Nordbloecke-Neues-Kreuzberger-Zentrum-03-2017a.jpg, 25 March 2017, own work on Wikimedia Commons; CC BY-SA 4.0. This photograph was an architectural input for the shallow NKZ curve and facade rhythm.

Changes to the photographic references: the scene, viewpoint, surface texture, lighting and colours were artistically reinterpreted with OpenAI ImageGen, and the facade was then revised using both photographs. Adobe Firefly Upscaler enlarged the resulting 1086 × 1448 pixel artwork to 4344 × 5792 pixels, synthetically enhancing fine detail. For the 50 × 70 cm version, a uniform 3:4 to 5:7 crop removed 4.762% of the original width from the two sides combined, retaining the full image height without stretching. The 30 × 40 cm composition is unchanged. alt: A red and cream S-Bahn train on the curved brick viaduct at Hackescher Markt seen from above, with a pale blue line beneath the arches. Hackescher Markt Berlin appears below.
visualCreditsHtml:
Artwork made for Walk of Berlin from my own concept image, created with the built-in ImageGen tool in OpenAI Codex. Enlarged for print with Adobe Firefly Upscaler, then retouched locally: small stray marks removed and the two-line title reset in Space Grotesk. It is a stylised illustration, not a measured map or an architectural drawing. The arches, tracks and surrounding blocks are simplified, and the pale blue line stands for the filled former moat, not open water.

Facts: the station and the line towards Alexanderplatz were built on the filled bed of the former fortress moat, from my own research for Walk of Berlin, based on the monument record for S-Bahnhof Hackescher Markt in the Berlin Denkmaldatenbank (Landesdenkmalamt Berlin) and period railway engineering reports of 1884 and 1885. The street name Am Zwirngraben was checked in November 2026. The curve of the line was compared with OpenStreetMap data (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL).

Lettering: Space Grotesk by Florian Karsten, SIL Open Font License 1.1.

The room image and the room video are 3D styling visualisations rendered in Blender with Poly Haven models and textures (CC0). Both show the 30 x 40 cm print in an oak frame. Frame, furniture and decor are not included.
